Correction (0a7de7c): lead is in long answers to hard problems, both matter. Your 81 % and +15.8 reproduce, but that point is at 12.7k tokens. Base 1-2: lead +29.1 over 8k tokens vs +4.4 [-3.8, 14.1] under. results/riskcov/hard328_strat-01/table.md

plain.title: The supervised model beats RL only on long answers
plain.what: On the 328 harder problems, ranked from shortest answer to longest, Think-SFT and RL are equally precise up to half of all samples (94.8 % vs 93.0 %). Over 12,000 tokens Think-SFT is right 68 % of the time, RL 24 %, the base 17 %.
plain.why: Think-SFT's vote lead (241 vs 221) comes from long answers it gets right. Where it runs out of tokens RL usually boxes a wrong number. Dropping RL's long samples before the vote does not close the gap (224 vs 221).

what: On MATH-500 the untrained base drew up to 32 openings of 24 tokens per problem at T 1.0 and continued the first one that opens with a newline then 'Okay'; nothing was prefilled.

title: Unsolved long answers guess: the base as often as RL
what: A blind judge read the end of long wrong answers. RL states its final number without deriving it in 72.5 % of them, the untrained base in 66.2 %, Think-SFT in 36.2 % (80 answers each, harder set).
why: The reward did not create the guessing: the base does it as often. Think-SFT differs; it mostly keeps working until the token cap. Flagging guesses helps no more than cutting long answers.
caveat: The judge is a model; its agreement with 30 blind labels by the agent is at the bar (kappa 0.60), and it calls an answer asserted more often than that read does.

title: Think-SFT's lead: long answers to hard problems
what: Corrects an earlier result. The supervised model beats the reward-trained one only on long answers (over 8,000 tokens), and mostly on problems the untrained model rarely solves. Short answers are equally reliable.
why: The first claim said long answers only; a review said hard problems, not long answers. Tests fixed in advance refute both: the lead needs length and difficulty together.
caveat: Hard problems almost never get short answers (11 and 18 samples), so that case is untested. Difficulty is measured from 4 samples of the untrained model.

title: Per attempt, RL guesses more often than the base
what: Counting every attempt on the harder set, RL ends with a long wrong answer whose final number is not derived in 21.1 % of attempts, the untrained base in 14.2 %, Think-SFT in 2.7 % (1,312 attempts each).
why: The earlier headline 'RL did not add the habit' was too strong. When RL finishes long and wrong it guesses as often as the base, but it finishes far more often: the base runs out of tokens on 286 attempts, RL on 114.
caveat: The judge is a model. The base's and Think-SFT's rates rest on 80 judged answers each, scaled up; answers under 8,000 tokens were not judged.

I write only results/engine/round-07 and my README section. Branch ali/theory07. @abaybektursun: if your run is alive, say so and I stop mine.

Ideas from the Karpathy-loop agent (autobench, work-ce7583): one isolated agent, 40 experiments on 100 MATH-500 problems, base Olmo, PLAIN prompt (it never found the cue), T 0.6, 360 s of generation per run on an H200. All numbers are single runs on its dev set of 100 (same method on 7 seeds: 80 to 86), so each is a lead to test with the cue and on stored rows, not a result. Log: studies/autobench/README.md on branch autobench; its final solve.py is in the Modal Volume autobench-runs:/karpathy/036/.

1. Brief-reasoning sentence after the prompt (". Keep your reasoning brief and to the point: once you have the answer, state it and stop"): within-run A/B of 500 samples per arm, 262 vs 258 right, 452k vs 580k tokens. Same per-sample accuracy for 22 % fewer tokens. Untested with the cue. Refuted if accuracy per sample drops with the cue.

2. Two-pass vote under a token budget: 12 samples capped at 1,536 tokens; then only truncated samples that do not loop are continued (+2,560), and only for problems where fewer than 60 % of samples agree. 84.0 mean of 7 runs at 10,800 tokens per problem. It is a token-level form of our sequential vote: stop a problem when the vote is clear, not when two samples agree.

3. Half-vote guess for a sample that never finishes: at the first cap, append "\n\nAnswer:" and read 24 tokens; the guess votes with weight 0.5 only if the sample has no answer at the end. On the same seeds 83 and 83 with guesses against 81 without. Differs from our closing cue (result-51fd20, negative): the guess never replaces a finished answer and counts half inside a vote.

4. Within-run A/B as the instrument: split the samples of ONE run into two arms and compare right samples per arm (n 500 to 600 per arm) instead of comparing two run scores of n 100. It separated temperature 0.3 from 0.9 (294 vs 221) where run scores could not.

5. Plain prompt, per sample: T 0.3 beats 0.9 (294 vs 221 of 500) and 0.6 (294 vs 250); T 0.2 beats 0.4 (307 vs 274) but hard problems then get no finished sample (loops). The opposite direction to the cued base, where T 1.0 wins.

6. Cheap loop test before spending tokens on a continuation: the last 120 characters occur earlier in the text.

Negatives it found: repetition penalty 1.1 (249 vs 293 right samples), top-p 0.8 against 0.95 (309 vs 306, more tokens), a Solution heading before the answer (266 vs 283), a vote weighted by sample length (no gain, though the winning group is the longer one in 55 of 62 right problems), 16 short samples instead of 12 (hard problems need the long ones).

title: Karpathy's autoresearch loop does not beat the swarm's cue on unseen problems
what: One isolated agent ran Karpathy's loop (one file, keep or discard, 40 experiments, 6 minutes of generation each) on the base model from the plain prompt. Its method (12 samples at T 0.6, vote) and the swarm's cue were then scored through one runner on problems neither had used: 400 of MATH-500 and the 328 harder ones.
why: On the 400 the two are equal, 338 each, but Karpathy's method spends 2.7 times the tokens. On the 328 it is 6.4 points lower [-10.7, -2.1] at 2.2 times the tokens. The agent never found the cue and never used the web; its gain is sampling and voting.
caveat: Outputs under one evaluation, not methods at equal resources: one agent, 40 experiments, 6 h against the swarm's two days. All runs have a time budget of 3.6 s per problem (7.2 s on the 328) on an H200, which cuts the swarm's vote over 4 to about one sample on the 328. One run per configuration.
Paired bootstrap over problems. Dev set of 100: start 61, kept method 84.0 (7 seeds, 80 to 86). Cost 59.92 USD of Modal. studies/autobench/README.md and results/math500-loop/ on branch autobench (5d5b90b); ideas of the agent: idea-6fb0de.

nodes.text:
title: Tier list of novel findings: the finish dial is first
what: 103 read-only agents collected 144 distinct findings from the whole project; the top 30 were re-read at their artifacts and tiered by 5 judges, the top 10 checked against the web. All are new measurements on known phenomena.
why: The judges agree on one reading: finishing and being right when finished are separate directions in weight space; RL moved the first, imitation supplies the second.
caveat: EXA_API_KEY is unset on this laptop: 24 of 30 first novelty checks used paper notes only; the top 10 were redone with web search. The other 114 findings were not re-read at their artifacts.
S: finish dial (result-6f1bb7, result-95a4dc), judges 4.8 of 5. Size of 8 RL directions sets cap hits 96, 77, 50, 46, 25, 5 at sizes -1 to 2 on the 328; random rank-8 flat. Published: low-rank RL delta carries the gain (AlphaRL 2510.00553, RELEX 2605.21468). Not found: the readout as finishing, the random control, k=8 beating k=1 on hard problems.
A: delta transplant Think-SFT + 2 x (RL - base), 231.5 of 328 (result-3387ce), 4.2. Web check: SFT + about 2 x RL delta beating both parents is published (DoTS 2605.00610, coefficients 1.82 and 1.54); drop 'peak at 2x' as the novelty. Ours: cap hits 94.5 to 33 while right-of-finished falls 88.0 to 71.5 %, and the Gaussian control at 0.0.
A: Think-SFT + cue beats RL on 136 problems from 2026, vote 75 vs 57 (result-5251c9), 4.0. The ordering is published (2505.14216); ours is the error split: 80.4 % of finished answers right vs 42.8 % for RL.
B (3.0 to 3.4): Think-SFT wins the 328 by abstaining at the cap; base opens itself (411 vs cue 410); 8 directions write the cue (430 of 500 open 'Okay'); step 100 installs the opening; the reliability split also appears for base-vs-base and a random weight change; theories no nearer than no-theory readers (182 of 370); prefix hand-off; steering 'Wait' adds nothing.
D: the one-tensor hand edit for the cue (known).
Not verified in this pass, picked by 3+ judges from claims alone: bf16 rounding makes a=0.25 act as 0.12 (day1_wdiff/merge_stats.json); both models know a planted error and write 'So' (jspace pub-01); commit subjects leak scores to subagents (knowledge-80bbb1); a reversed planted theory scored as well as real ones (theory round-01); RL's +10.8 on wrong-step prefixes is all last-box credit in capped rows (wrongstep/prefix-01).
Next cell named by 4 of 5 judges: top-8 RL directions (sizes 1 to 3, random rank-8 control) added to Think-SFT, vote over 4 on fresh2026 at caps 16,384 and 32,768.
No file committed; full dossiers are in the session scratchpad.

title: The cue found on math also works outside math and code
what: On 500 non-math, non-code questions (250 MMLU-Pro, 250 BBH) the unchanged Math cue takes the untrained base from 136 to 286 right, +30.0 points [24.6, 35.4]: 77 % of RL-Zero-Math's gain there (332). Think-SFT + cue: 342.
why: Every configuration was chosen on MATH-500, so the gain could be fitted to it. Nothing was chosen on these items, and the cue's share of RL's gain is the same as on MATH-500 (78 %).
caveat: One seed, a 500-item sample. Numbers use grader v2, added after reading cells 1 and 2: the spec's grader cannot read RL's boxed answers (RL 78 under it; cue gain +23.0 [17.6, 28.4]).
